slides.text: In the courtroom, Marcus Vance and I are mortal enemies. We are the two sharpest divorce litigators in Manhattan, spending forty hours a week tearing each other’s prenuptial clauses to shreds in tailored charcoal suits. Neither of us knew we lived two blocks apart—until I walked into the 24-hour coin laundromat at 1:15 AM on a Thursday in faded flannel pajamas and found him separating his delicates.

We stared at each other in horrified silence over a basket of mismatched socks. Then we struck an unspoken truce: between 1:00 and 2:30 AM beside the humming dryers, the law didn't exist. He lent me quarters when the change machine jammed; I taught him how to get espresso stains out of silk ties. Stripped of our courtroom armor, he was funny, exhausted, and hopelessly tender.

Last Friday, after a brutal six-hour hearing where we argued over a billionaire’s yacht, the judge called a recess. Marcus walked across the aisle, solemnly handed me a sealed legal exhibit envelope in front of twenty paralegals, and whispered, 'Counselor, you dropped this.' Inside the manila folder was my missing left cashmere sock, warm from the dryer, folded around a note: 'Dinner tonight. No objections allowed.'
